title: Why Your Review Score Has Almost Nothing to Do With Your Rooms
author: Jonathan Bush
excerpt: Cornell research found that 70% of negative reviews trace back to a communication failure, not a service failure. Here's why checkout is the wrong moment to ask for feedback — and what changes when someone asks earlier.
body:
Here's a number that should bother anyone running a hotel: seventy percent of negative reviews trace back to a communication failure, not a service failure. Not dirty rooms. Not slow check-in. A guest who had a problem and never told anyone about it.

That's a Cornell research finding, and it's worth sitting with, because it means most of what's tanking your review score isn't happening in the room. It's happening in the silence after something went wrong.

What “communication failure” actually means

It sounds abstract until you picture the specific guest. Say the shower runs cold for the first thirty seconds. Say the pillow's too thin. Say housekeeping missed the extra towels. None of these are disasters. None of them are worth walking down to the front desk over.

So the guest doesn't. They just note it, quietly, the way people note small disappointments they've decided aren't worth the effort of fixing. And then they check out, and somewhere on the drive home or the flight back, the note becomes a sentence in a review. By then, the moment to actually help them is long gone.

The property never failed at service. It failed at hearing about the problem while there was still time to do something about it.

Checkout is the wrong moment to ask

Most hotels ask for feedback at exactly the point where feedback can no longer change anything: after checkout, in a survey nobody particularly wants to fill out, about a stay that's already over.

By then, the guest has made up their mind. The review, if there is one, is really just a record of a decision that happened days earlier, in a room, in silence.

The window that actually matters is earlier — night one or two, while the guest is still there and something can still change. A guest who mentions the cold shower on night one gets a fixed shower on night two. A guest who never gets asked writes about the cold shower three days later, and there's nothing anyone can do with that information except read it.

What changes when someone actually asks in time

Properties that build in a mid-stay check-in — a simple, low-friction way for a guest to flag something while they're still there to benefit from the fix — see satisfaction scores climb 14 to 25 percent. Review volume goes up 40 to 60 percent, not because more guests are unhappy, but because more of them are being heard before disappointment calcifies into a review.

The staff isn't doing anything fundamentally different. Same training, same standards, same people who were always capable of fixing a cold shower or finding an extra pillow. What changed is that someone finally asked the question early enough for the answer to matter.

Three things worth taking with you

  1. The complaint you never heard is the one costing you. The guest who says nothing isn't satisfied — they've just decided it isn't worth mentioning. That's not the same thing, and the gap between the two is where your review score actually lives.
  2. Timing matters more than tone. It's not about asking guests nicely for feedback. It's about asking early enough that the feedback can still change their stay, not just your data.
  3. This isn't a bigger ask — it's a better-timed one. You don't need a longer survey or a more elaborate process. You need one small question, sent at the right moment, to the right guest, while there's still time to act on the answer.

And here's the gift — an actual message you can send tonight:

“Just checking in — is there anything about your stay so far we could take care of before you check out?”

One line. Sent on night one or two, not at checkout. It costs nothing to ask and gives the guest somewhere to put the small thing they'd otherwise have carried home and turned into a review.
